record.original_question: What rigorous mathematical definitions of emergence and emergent properties are needed for biology so that higher-level biological behavior can be characterized and explained in a mathematically usable way without requiring exhaustive reduction to lower-level constituents?

evidence.quote: For this, rigorous mathematical definitions of emergence and emergent properties are required, and while there are some initial considerations [99, 93], further work is required.
By identifying emergent phenomena we can explain the properties of a biological system without the limitations of accounting for the complexity of the underlying constituents.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Formulate a rigorous mathematical framework for the notion of "emergence" applicable to biological systems. Specifically, provide precise definitions of the following:

1. A formal notion of a multi-level system, consisting of a "lower-level" mathematical model (e.g., a state space X with dynamics, possibly stochastic, describing interacting constituents) and a "higher-level" description (a quotient or coarse-grained space Y together with observables and dynamics on Y).

2. A definition of an "emergent property" of such a system — a property P of the higher-level description Y such that:
   (a) P is well-defined and can be analyzed purely in terms of the higher-level dynamics, without requiring the explicit reconstruction of trajectories or states at the lower level;
   (b) P is not trivially reducible to a property of an individual constituent, in a sense to be made precise (e.g., P depends on the joint state in a way that cannot be expressed as an average or sum of single-constituent properties);
   (c) P is robust under a specified class of perturbations or refinements of the lower-level model.

3. Criteria under which the higher-level model faithfully represents the lower-level model with respect to emergent properties (e.g., commutativity of coarse-graining with time evolution up to controlled error).

The problem is to give such definitions that are mathematically usable — meaning theorems can be stated and proved about when emergent properties exist, are unique, are computable from the higher-level model alone, and how they relate to lower-level dynamics — and that apply meaningfully to biological examples (such as pattern formation, collective motion, or homeostasis).
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a foundational conceptual/definitional problem in mathematical biology and complex systems. While there are partial proposals (e.g., causal emergence frameworks by Hoel, integrated information theory, and coarse-graining approaches), no single rigorous, universally accepted mathematical definition of emergence for biological systems exists. The problem is widely regarded as open.

status_evidence.title: When the Map Is Better Than the Territory (Hoel)
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes a measure of causal emergence via effective information at coarse-grained scales.
status_evidence.claim: Partial frameworks for quantifying emergence exist but are not universally adopted.

status_evidence.title: Reconciling emergences: An information-theoretic approach (Rosas et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Develops information-theoretic criteria for causal and downward-causation emergence.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple competing mathematical proposals for emergence exist; no consensus rigorous definition for biology.
